# Wirecard Public-Fraud Trail: Evidence-Bounded Reconstruction

## Executive summary

The returned evidence supports a limited but coherent reconstruction of the Wirecard public-fraud trail.

On 28 April 2020, Wirecard AG publicly announced that KPMG had delivered a special-investigation report. Wirecard characterized that report as finding no incriminating evidence for public allegations of balance-sheet forgery and no significant findings requiring adjustment of the 2016–2018 annual accounts. At the same time, Wirecard acknowledged that, under KPMG’s increased forensic requirements, not all data needed to prove revenues for the relevant years could be obtained because the data were primarily controlled by third parties. Wirecard also disclosed documentation and organizational weaknesses and postponed publication of its annual accounts and annual press conference, stating that it would coordinate with EY concerning completion of audit measures. [SRC-001 — Wirecard AG: KPMG delivers report on special investigation](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation)

A European Parliament Economic Governance Support Unit study, written by external authors, reached a broader supervisory assessment. It stated that all five lines of defense against corporate fraud and deception had failed “in one way or another”: Wirecard’s internal controls, supervisory board, external audit, financial-reporting and auditing oversight bodies, and BaFin as market supervisor. The document expressly presents these as the authors’ opinions rather than an official position of the European Parliament or BaFin. [SRC-002 — What are the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case?](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf)

The returned evidence does **not** establish the whereabouts or absence of any specific cash balance, the existence or status of a €1.9 billion trustee-account balance, the wording of EY’s audit opinion or warnings, detailed actions by BaFin or other regulators, or any fact concerning Jan Marsalek’s disappearance. Those issues therefore remain unresolved within the source-bounded record.

## Scope and evidentiary limits

Only two substantive sources were returned by the benchmark tools:

- Wirecard’s 28 April 2020 corporate disclosure concerning the KPMG special investigation.
- The European Parliament Economic Governance Support Unit study on the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case.

The record does not include the full KPMG report, EY audit communications, bank confirmations, trustee-account records, a detailed Bundestag investigation, an ESMA peer-review report, official wanted notices, prosecutor findings, or evidence concerning Marsalek’s location.

Accordingly, the report distinguishes among:

- **Verified source facts:** what the returned documents expressly state.
- **Corporate assertions:** statements made by Wirecard about KPMG’s work, its own controls, or its own data.
- **External assessments:** conclusions in the policy study, attributed to its authors.
- **Inferences:** limited conclusions drawn from the relationship between the source statements.
- **Unresolved uncertainty:** matters not established by the returned evidence.

No fact is inferred merely because it appeared in a search query or is commonly associated with the Wirecard case.

## Chronology supported by the returned evidence

### 2016–2018: Annual accounts and TPA revenue period

Wirecard’s disclosure refers to audits of the annual accounts for 2016–2018 and to the proof of revenues in its Third Party Acquiring business, or TPA. Wirecard stated that no significant findings had been made that required adjustment of those annual accounts. This is a statement by Wirecard describing the KPMG investigation; the returned material does not contain the underlying KPMG report. [SRC-001](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation)

### Since 2019: Claimed compliance remediation

Wirecard stated that KPMG had identified documentation and organizational weaknesses during the audit period, although Wirecard said those weaknesses had already been identified internally. Wirecard further stated that it had been addressing them since 2019 by establishing a Global Compliance Organization and receiving support from external consultants. [SRC-001](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation)

This establishes a corporate claim that remediation began in 2019. The returned source does not identify the weaknesses, the consultants, the organization’s powers, or whether the remediation was effective.

### December 2019: Data supplied for forensic review

Wirecard stated that it had provided KPMG with more than “200 mio” data sets relating to December 2019. It said the resulting forensic audit had revealed no deviations between reported revenues and account balances. [SRC-001](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation)

The source does not clarify whether “200 mio” means 200 million records, transactions, data points, or another unit. It also does not establish that this review resolved evidence limitations concerning the 2016–2018 period.

### 28 April 2020: KPMG report and Wirecard disclosure

Wirecard stated that it received KPMG’s special-audit report in the early hours of 28 April 2020. The disclosure was dated 28 April 2020 at 07:52 CET/CEST and was presented as inside information under Article 17 of the EU Market Abuse Regulation. DGAP transmitted the announcement, while Wirecard stated that it was solely responsible for its content. [SRC-001](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation)

Wirecard said the KPMG report would be published as soon as possible on its transparency website.

### 30 April 2020: Annual accounts and press conference postponed

Wirecard announced that the release of its annual accounts and its annual press conference would not take place on 30 April 2020. It said that it would coordinate with EY concerning completion of audit measures, taking account of COVID-19-related restrictions and completion of the KPMG report. [SRC-001](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation)

The returned evidence does not provide the subsequent EY audit opinion or explain precisely why the audit measures remained incomplete.

### May and November 2020: Policy-study dates

The supervisory policy study states that its manuscript was completed in May 2020 and is labeled “PE 651.385 – November 2020 EN.” It was requested by the European Parliament’s Committee on Economic and Monetary Affairs. [SRC-002](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf)

## Wirecard’s public statements

### KPMG’s alleged finding concerning balance-sheet forgery

Wirecard stated:

> “Incriminating evidence for the public allegations of balance sheet forgery has not been identified.”

This is a **corporate characterization** of the KPMG investigation, not an independently verified conclusion in the returned evidence. The full KPMG report is not included, so the source record does not permit an assessment of the report’s methodology, qualifications, reservations, or scope limitations. [SRC-001](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation)

### The four areas identified by Wirecard

Wirecard stated that the investigation covered four areas:

1. Third Party Acquiring.
2. Merchant Cash Advance/Digital Lending.
3. Business activities in India.
4. Business activities in Singapore.

Wirecard said that no significant findings had been made requiring adjustment of the 2016–2018 annual accounts. Again, this is Wirecard’s account of the investigation rather than the complete text of KPMG’s findings. [SRC-001](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation)

### Revenue evidence and third-party data control

Wirecard stated that the documents and audit measures available during the 2016–2018 annual-account audits were sufficient to prove TPA revenues. It simultaneously acknowledged that KPMG’s increased forensic requirements could not be fully met because not all required data could be obtained and the data were primarily controlled by third parties. [SRC-001](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation)

This creates an important evidentiary tension:

- Wirecard defended the sufficiency of the earlier audit documentation and procedures.
- Wirecard acknowledged that KPMG could not obtain all data it considered necessary to prove revenues for the relevant years.

The returned source does not explain whether the difference resulted from a different audit approach, a higher forensic evidence threshold, changes in data availability, or another factor.

### December 2019 reported revenues and account balances

Wirecard stated that the December 2019 forensic audit had found no deviations between reported revenues and account balances. This is a corporate statement about the result of a data review. It does not, by itself, establish:

- that all historical revenues were verified;
- that cash existed in any specified amount;
- that bank or trustee balances were independently confirmed;
- that the 2016–2018 evidence limitations were resolved.

Those conclusions are not supported by the returned material.

## Audit uncertainty and auditor warnings

### KPMG

The evidence supports the following limited conclusions about KPMG:

- KPMG conducted a special investigation for Wirecard.
- Wirecard said KPMG delivered its report on 28 April 2020.
- Wirecard characterized the report as finding no incriminating evidence for public allegations of balance-sheet forgery.
- Wirecard said no significant findings required adjustment of the 2016–2018 annual accounts.
- Wirecard acknowledged that not all data required to prove revenues under KPMG’s increased forensic requirements could be obtained.
- Wirecard said KPMG identified documentation and organizational weaknesses.

[SRC-001](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation)

The returned evidence does not establish whether KPMG issued a qualification, disclaimer, reservation, warning, or adverse conclusion. It also does not identify the exact data KPMG requested or explain the significance of the missing information.

### EY

The source refers to EY as “E&Y” and identifies it as the auditor with which Wirecard would coordinate concerning completion of audit measures. [SRC-001](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation)

No EY audit opinion, warning, qualification, disclaimer, evidence request, bank-confirmation issue, or conclusion about cash is included in the returned material. Therefore, no specific EY warning or failure can be reported as a source-supported fact.

### Audit oversight

The policy study identifies external audit and the oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing as two of the five defense lines that, in the authors’ assessment, failed in one way or another. [SRC-002](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf)

That broad assessment does not supply a detailed chronology of audit communications or identify a particular act or omission by an individual auditor or oversight body.

## The alleged missing cash

### What is established

The returned evidence establishes only that Wirecard referred to “reported revenues and account balances” and said that the December 2019 forensic audit found no deviations between them. [SRC-001](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation)

### What is not established

The returned sources do not establish:

- a specific amount of allegedly missing cash;
- the existence of a €1.9 billion balance;
- trustee accounts or escrow accounts;
- the identity of a trustee or bank;
- bank confirmations;
- whether any balance was physically or electronically present;
- whether cash was held for Wirecard or a subsidiary;
- whether a bank, auditor, trustee, regulator, or investigator verified the funds;
- whether the funds were absent, misrepresented, inaccessible, transferred, frozen, or otherwise unavailable.

The search queries sought evidence about these issues, but the returned excerpts did not contain it. Therefore, the whereabouts or alleged absence of required cash remains unresolved in this report.

### Evidentiary distinction

It would be incorrect to treat Wirecard’s statement about reported revenues and account balances as proof that cash itself had been independently verified. The source does not say that the balances were confirmed by a bank or trustee, nor does it describe the underlying evidence.

## Supervisory and regulatory failures

### Status of the supervisory assessment

The second source is a policy study produced for the European Parliament’s Economic Governance Support Unit and requested by the ECON Committee. Its authors are identified as Katja Langenbucher, Christian Leuz, Jan Pieter Krahnen, and Loriana Pelizzon. [SRC-002](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf)

The document expressly states that the opinions are the sole responsibility of the authors and do not necessarily represent the official position of the European Parliament. It also states that Katja Langenbucher’s opinions do not reflect a position taken by BaFin, although she is identified as a member of BaFin’s Supervisory Board. [SRC-002](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf)

The supervisory conclusions must therefore be labeled as **authorial assessments**, not official findings attributed to the European Parliament or BaFin.

### The five lines of defense

The authors state that all five lines of defense against corporate fraud and deception failed “in one way or another”:

1. Wirecard’s internal control system.
2. Wirecard’s supervisory board.
3. Wirecard’s external audit.
4. Oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing.
5. BaFin as market supervisor.

[SRC-002](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf)

The study describes the slow unraveling of Wirecard as surprising because, in the authors’ view, signals suggesting fraudulent behavior had existed for years. It identifies what it calls a flawed market and institutional oversight architecture as a root cause and concludes that the existing architecture was not sufficiently fit to preserve market integrity and investor protection. [SRC-002](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf)

These are broad assessments. The returned excerpt does not document every alleged signal, identify each responsible actor, or provide a detailed event-by-event account of the failures.

### Proposed reforms

The study recommends:

- stronger accountability;
- better information flow to markets and supervisors;
- continued recognition of whistleblowing and short selling as information sources;
- stronger incentives for external auditors to detect manipulation and fraud;
- legally required effective internal-control systems for listed firms;
- reporting by the head of internal control to the supervisory board rather than management;
- consideration of internal-control audits;
- stronger BaFin supervisory and enforcement powers, including forensic and investigative tools;
- reducing self-regulatory bodies such as FREP to a purely ancillary, optional function.

[SRC-002](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf)

These are policy recommendations, not evidence that each proposed reform was legally required at the time or that each identified institution committed a specific documented act.

### Other named institutions

The study’s abbreviation list names a number of regulators and oversight bodies, including BaFin, FREP, ESMA, the FCA, AMF, CONSOB, the FRC, H3C, PCAOB, SEC, PRA, and others. [SRC-002](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf)

However, an institution’s appearance in an abbreviation list does not establish that it had a particular relationship with Wirecard or committed a particular failure. The returned excerpt specifically supports BaFin’s identification as the market supervisor and FREP’s identification as Germany’s Financial Reporting Enforcement Panel. It does not support detailed claims about the conduct of every institution listed.

## Jan Marsalek’s disappearance

The returned evidence contains no source-supported fact about:

- the date or circumstances of Jan Marsalek’s disappearance;
- his last known location;
- any official wanted notice;
- an Interpol notice;
- prosecutor findings;
- reported sightings;
- alleged travel or destination;
- his current status;
- assistance by another person or entity;
- conclusions from Bellingcat, a Bundestag investigation, or another investigative body.

The search queries sought such information, but the returned excerpts did not provide it. The only defensible conclusion is that Marsalek’s disappearance is unresolved within the available evidence.

No relationship between Marsalek and any named individual, regulator, bank, intelligence service, or other entity should be added to the reconstruction.

## Overall assessment

The source-bounded trail has four supported components:

1. **A public corporate defense.** Wirecard said KPMG had found no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery and no significant findings requiring adjustment of the 2016–2018 accounts.
2. **An acknowledged evidence problem.** Wirecard also admitted that not all data needed under KPMG’s increased forensic requirements could be obtained because relevant data were primarily controlled by third parties.
3. **A delayed audit and reporting process.** Wirecard postponed its annual accounts and press conference and referred to ongoing coordination with EY.
4. **A broad external supervisory critique.** A European Parliament policy study assessed that all five lines of defense had failed in some way and called for substantial reforms.

The evidence does not permit a complete reconstruction of the alleged cash shortfall, a definitive account of auditor warnings, a detailed regulatory chronology, or Jan Marsalek’s disappearance. The strongest supported conclusion is therefore not a complete factual narrative of the fraud, but a documented conflict between Wirecard’s public characterization of the KPMG review and the evidentiary limitations that Wirecard itself acknowledged, alongside an external assessment that the surrounding control and supervisory architecture had failed.
